newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - German March jobless won't ease EMU task.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - German March jobless won't ease EMU task.

text.p: News that German unemployment fell in March from February's 64-year record, while welcome, still offered little comfort to a government struggling to ready its economy for Europe's single currency, analysts said on Monday.

Unadjusted unemployment fell to 4.48 million in March, down 190,000 from February but still 340,000 higher than a year earlier, sources who had gained access to data from the Federal Labour Office told Reuters.

The sources said unemployment in western Germany fell to around 3.13 million from 3.26 million in February. In the ex-communist east the jobless total was 1.35 million, down from 1.41 million in the previous month.
The Labour office was due to release official jobless data on Tuesday, but the Bild newspaper confirmed the leaked figures in a report released ahead of publication on Tuesday.
Bild said the unadjusted unemployment rate fell to 11.7 percent in March from 12.2 percent in February.

Analysts said the headline number pointed to a fall in the seasonally-adjusted figure of 15,000 to 25,000 from February's 4.32 million -- too small to compensate for a huge winter jobs shakeout which hit the depressed construction sector.
The adjusted figure would still be a post-war record for the month of March, Wilhelm Adamy, labour market expert of the German trades union congress (DGB) told Reuters.
Gernot Nerb at Salomon Brothers in Frankfurt said: "This is a relatively modest improvement, and the new jobs will have come almost exclusively from the construction sector.
"People are being hired back into the building sector, but not as fast as they were laid off. We can expect this effect to fade over the next few months."
Economist Holger Fahrinkrug at UBS in Frankfurt echoed that view: "Any decline is good, but this is largely in line with the consensus," he said.
Forecasts by 10 economists polled last week by Reuters showed expectations of a seasonal decline of up to 85,000, to flat at the other end. Most foresaw a decline of about 50,000.
Unadjusted unemployment is the most politically sensitive jobs number in Germany, and directly impacts on Bonn's ability to rein in borrowing and qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
Analysts said it would be difficult to get unemployment down to the government's target of an average 4.2 million this year -- up 200,000 on the 1996 average.
Every extra 100,000 people on the dole is estimated to cost the state budget four billion marks in extra benefit payments and lost tax revenues.
Analysts said that problem may account for a perceived softening in Finance Minister Theo Waigel's call for a strict reading of EMU's guiding Maastricht treaty.
The treaty stipulates that countries wanting to take part should have a budget deficit of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) this year to join EMU in 1999.

Waigel has said in the past that countries must hit the three percent figure exactly to join, but two British dailies, the Guardian and the Financial Times, reported he had shifted his stance at the weekend. They quoted him saying: "I have never nailed myself to the cross of three percent".
The minister, commenting on Monday in Munich, termed the press reports "unfair in the highest degree" and a spokeswoman said there had been no change in his position.
Waigel has warned, however, that cuts in welfare payments and possibly tax increases would be needed by the summer if Germany is to hit its borrowing target.
Fahrinkrug said he still expected government efforts to fall short of the mark. "It will be very hard to push through cuts social in social spending this year," he said.
Still, he expects Germany to be in the starting line-up for EMU, even if its deficit is 3.1 or 3.2 percent of GDP.
-- Bonn newsroom, 49-228-26097150
